The recovery has revived a housing project initiated in 2012 but abandoned after the original developer failed to complete the development, leaving the bank with a non-performing loan and a stranded property for about 10 years.
Managing director and chief executive officer of FMBN, Shehu Usman Osidi, disclosed this on Wednesday during an inspection of the recovered property in Abuja, attributing the breakthrough to the ICPC’s intervention and collaboration among government institutions.
According to him, the anti-corruption agency facilitated the recovery through a court-ordered forfeiture, which subsequently returned the property to the bank for its original purpose of providing residential accommodation.
He explained that the court also mandated the ICPC to supervise the process and ensure that the property was developed for housing, rather than remain abandoned or diverted from its intended public purpose.
Osidi disclosed that a new developer had presented a proposal to deliver 1,358 housing units on the recovered property, representing an increase of 396 homes over the 962 units originally envisaged when the project commenced in 2012.
The proposed expansion, he said, presents an opportunity to turn a failed housing investment into a larger residential development, potentially extending homeownership opportunities to more Nigerians.
The FMBN chief noted that the project had remained on the bank’s books as a non-performing loan for about 10 years following the failure of the original developer, highlighting the financial and developmental consequences of abandoned housing investments.
He commended the ICPC for its diligence in pursuing the case and facilitating the recovery, saying the intervention had helped protect public investment and restore the prospect of delivering the homes originally intended for Nigerians.
The recovery comes amid Nigeria’s persistent housing deficit, with millions of citizens struggling to access decent and affordable accommodation due to rising construction costs, limited mortgage financing and inadequate housing supply.
It also underscores the need for stronger monitoring of housing projects financed with public funds, effective enforcement of development agreements and timely intervention when developers fail to meet their obligations.
Osidi maintained that the recovery demonstrated how collaboration among government institutions could help safeguard public assets, address longstanding financial setbacks and restore stalled development projects for the benefit of Nigerians.
